claim: Many pathogens possess the capacity for sex through outcrossing, despite being able to reproduce also asexually and/or via selfing.
source: Many pathogens possess the capacity for sex through outcrossing, despite being able to reproduce also asexually and/or via selfing.
evidence: This is a general statement about pathogen reproductive strategies that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Populations supporting high levels of coinfection result in hotspots of novel genetic diversity.
source: Populations supporting high levels of coinfection –a prerequisite of sex – result in hotspots of novel genetic diversity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the analysis of field data and genotyping results.

claim: Pathogen populations supporting coinfection have a higher probability of surviving winter.
source: Pathogen populations supporting coinfection also have a higher probability of surviving winter.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on multi-year census data and statistical modeling.

claim: Individuals that undergo sexual reproduction transmit only half their genome per offspring produced in contrast to asexual and selfing individuals.
source: Individuals that undergo sexual reproduction transmit only half their genome per offspring produced in contrast to asexual and selfing individuals (Lehtonen et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Sexual outcrossing is assumed to provide both ecological and evolutionary advantages.
source: To counteract this two-fold cost of sex, sexual outcrossing is assumed to provide both ecological and evolutionary advantages (Otto, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claim: The Red Queen Hypothesis predicts sexual reproduction to be advantageous in the presence of coevolving parasites.
source: The Red Queen Hypothesis predicts sexual reproduction to be advantageous in the presence of coevolving parasites, as offspring that are genetically different from their parents should have higher fitness than non-sexual offspring (Bell, 1982; Hamilton, 1980; Lively, 2010).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by multiple citations.

claim: Empirical studies have demonstrated parasite mediated selection to explain the observed distribution of outcrossing in hosts.
source: In support of this prediction, empirical studies have demonstrated parasite mediated selection to explain the observed distribution of outcrossing in hosts (King et al., 2011; Wilson and Sherman, 2013; Lively, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Theoretically it has been possible to identify a parameter space where coevolution with the host favors sexual reproduction in the parasite.
source: Indeed, theoretically it has been possible to identify a parameter space where coevolution with the host favors sexual reproduction in the parasite (Howard and Lively, 2002; Galvani et al., 2003; Salathé et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The empirical evidence for advantages of sex in parasite populations are still few and conflicting.
source: However, the empirical evidence for such advantages of sex in parasite populations are still few and conflicting (Gouyon and de Vienne, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation assessing the state of empirical evidence.

claim: In free-living facultatively sexual organisms that alternate between asexual and sexual reproduction, the sexual offspring are often the dormant or dispersing life stages.
source: In free-living facultatively sexual organisms that alternate between asexual and sexual reproduction, the sexual offspring are often the dormant or dispersing life stages (Stelzer and Lehtonen, 2016; Simon et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In some of the most devastating fungal pathogens of crops, the spores that are produced via outcrossing are also those that are suitable for long-distance dispersal.
source: Similarly, in some of the most devastating fungal pathogens of crops, the spores that are produced via outcrossing are also those that are suitable for long-distance dispersal (Rieux et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Sexual spores in some fungal pathogens provide means of surviving unfavorable environmental conditions.
source: or provide means of surviving unfavorable environmental conditions (Billiard et al., 2012; Burt, 2000; Saleh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ability to outcross may be a key determinant of both the numeric and genetic composition of the next season's epidemic.
source: While sexual offspring do not contribute to current local population growth, the ability to outcross may be a key determinant of both the numeric and genetic composition of the next season's epidemic (Penczykowski et al., 2015; Tack and Laine, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For strategies where outcrossing is timed with low potential asexual growth, the cost of sex is expected to be reduced.
source: For such strategies where outscrossing is timed with low potential asexual growth, for example due to seasonality, the cost of sex is expected to be reduced (Gerber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claim: There is evidence of high rates of outcrossing in homothallic species.
source: Nonetheless, there is evidence of high rates of outcrossing in homothallic species (Billiard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Maintenance of selfing may be favored when mate availability is spatially and/or temporally variable.
source: Even when outcrossing is expected to provide short- or long-term advantages, maintenance of selfing may be favored when mate availability is spatially and/or temporally variable (Jarne and Charlesworth, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: For many pathogens, coinfection is the ecological prerequisite of sexual recombination.
source: For many pathogens, coinfection is the ecological prerequisite of sexual recombination, as outcrossing and hybridization take place during active infection of the same host individual by different strains (Froissart et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Coinfections have been widely reported for different pathogens.
source: Although coinfections have been widely reported for different pathogens, remarkably little is understood of the determinants of coinfection (Tollenaere et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Mixed reproductive strategies have been described for a wide range of pathogen species.
source: Mixed reproductive strategies have been described for a wide range of pathogen species (Billiard et al., 2012; Billiard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The sexual stage is methodologically notoriously difficult to study in many pathogens given their microscopic size and the fact that mating types cannot be identified morphologically.
source: However, the sexual stage is methodologically notoriously difficult to study in many pathogens given their microscopic size and the fact that mating types cannot be identified morphologically.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about methodological challenges in pathogen research.

claim: Sexual reproduction in pathogens may take place inside the host and may be triggered by specific environmental cues that are difficult to mimic under controlled experimental conditions.
source: Moreover, sexual reproduction may take place inside the host, and may be triggered by specific environmental cues that are difficult to mimic under controlled experimental conditions (Billiard et al., 2012; Tack and Laine, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Podosphaera plantaginis is a specialist powdery mildew fungus naturally infecting Plantago lanceolata.
source: Our analysis is based on data collected from Podosphaera plantaginis, a specialist powdery mildew fungus naturally infecting Plantago lanceolata.
evidence: This is a factual description of the study system based on established knowledge.

claim: The visually conspicuous symptoms caused by P. plantaginis enable accurate tracking of infection in the wild.
source: The visually conspicuous symptoms caused by P. plantaginis enable accurate tracking of infection in the wild.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of the study system based on established knowledge.

claim: P. plantaginis persists as a highly dynamic metapopulation with frequent extinctions and (re)colonizations of local populations.
source: Long-term epidemiological data across approximately 4000 local plant populations in the Åland Islands, southwest of Finland, have demonstrated this pathogen to persist as a highly dynamic metapopulation with frequent extinctions and (re)colonizations of local populations (Jousimo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Overwinter survival of local pathogen populations has proven to be the vulnerable life-history stage of P. plantaginis in Åland with a high fraction of the local pathogen populations going extinct.
source: Overwinter survival of local pathogen populations has proven to be the vulnerable life-history stage of P. plantaginis in Åland with a high fraction of the local pathogen populations going extinct (Jousimo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The pathogen survives the winter in resting structures, chasmothecia.
source: The pathogen survives the winter in resting structures, chasmothecia (Tack and Laine, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Chasmothecia are produced through sexual reproduction as the hyphal cells of one (selfing) or two strains (outcrossing) fuse when infecting the same host plant.
source: These resting structures are produced through sexual reproduction as the hyphal cells of one (selfing) or two strains (outcrossing) fuse when infecting the same host plant.
evidence: This is a description of the reproductive biology of the pathogen based on established knowledge.

claim: The diploid zygote undergoes meiotic division to yield haploid ascospores that develop inside the chasmothecium.
source: The resulting diploid zygote undergoes meiotic division to yield haploid ascospores that develop inside the chasmothecium.
evidence: This is a description of the reproductive biology of the pathogen based on established knowledge.

claim: At the onset of the growing season chasmothecia rupture, releasing the ascopores that initiate new infections.
source: At the onset of the growing season these chasmothecia rupture, releasing the ascopores that initiate new infections (Tollenaere and Laine, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: 619, 703, 693 and 833 pathogen populations were sampled in 2012–15 for genotyping.
source: We sampled 619, 703, 693 and 833 populations in 2012–15 for subsequent genotyping (Table S1).
evidence: This is a description of the data collection methods and sample sizes.

claim: Coinfection proved to be common yet spatially variable across the P. plantaginis metapopulation.
source: Coinfection proved to be common yet spatially variable across the P. plantaginis metapopulation (Figure 1A) (Susi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding based on the genotyping data and spatial analysis, with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: In all years approximately half of the pathogen populations supported at least one coinfected sample (45–58%).
source: In all years approximately half of the pathogen populations supported at least one coinfected sample, (45–58%; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding based on the genotyping data.

claim: Coinfection was more likely to be found in larger and more diverse pathogen populations.
source: We found that coinfection was more likely to be found in larger and more diverse pathogen populations (Significant positive effect of number of MLGs and infection abundance; Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical modeling presented in Table 1.

claim: Connectivity of pathogen populations had a positive, albeit not significant, effect on the probability of coinfection.
source: Connectivity of pathogen populations, which is considered a proxy for gene flow among populations as it is estimated from distances separating local pathogen populations (Jousimo et al., 2014), had a positive, albeit not significant, effect on the probability of coinfection (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical modeling presented in Table 1, with a citation for the connectivity measure.

claim: An already infected plant is more likely to be infected by another strain.
source: Our results show that an already infected plant is more likely to be infected by another strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the ABC analysis presented in the figure supplement.

claim: Coinfections were more common than expected by chance under the assumption that infections by different MLGs are statistically independent.
source: In other words, coinfections were more common than expected by chance under the assumption that infections by different MLGs are statistically independent.
evidence: This is a finding from the ABC analysis.

claim: The result that coinfections are more common than expected by chance was consistent in both years 2012 and 2013 (posterior probability 0.98 and 0.988, respectively).
source: The result was consistent in both years 2012 and 2013 (posterior probability 0.98 and 0.988, respectively; Figure 1—figure supplement 6)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the ABC analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: 182, 189, and 235 novel MLGs were identified in 2013–2015, respectively, when compared to MLGs detected the previous year.
source: When all located pathogen populations were genotyped, we identified 182, 189, and 235 novel MLGs in 2013–2015, respectively, when compared to MLGs detected the previous year (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding based on the genotyping data.

claim: The number of new MLGs at the population level increased with the prevalence of coinfection at the end of the previous epidemic season.
source: The number of new MLGs at the population level increased with the prevalence of coinfection at the end of the previous epidemic season which is the time when outcrossing takes place (Figure 1C; Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical modeling presented in Table 1 and Figure 1C.

claim: The prevalence of coinfection was a strong predictor of novel MLGs the following year even after controlling for the effects of local pathogen population size, diversity, pathogen population connectivity, and spatial and temporal autocorrelation.
source: The prevalence of coinfection was a strong predictor of novel MLGs the following year even after controlling for the effects of local pathogen population size, diversity (number of MLGs), pathogen population connectivity (proxy for gene flow) as well as spatial and temporal autocorrelation (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical modeling presented in Table 1.

claim: In pathogen populations where the prevalence of coinfection is high, the pathogen has a higher survival probability.
source: Using data from the natural pathogen metapopulation, we also found that in those pathogen populations where the prevalence of coinfection is high – and hence where sexual reproduction can take place – the pathogen has a higher survival probability (Table 1; Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical modeling presented in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: The effect of coinfection on successful overwintering is positive even after controlling for the effects of pathogen population size and diversity.
source: The effect of coinfection on successful overwintering is positive even after controlling for the effects of pathogen population size and diversity, which both increase survival probability.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical modeling.

claim: Resting spores were produced in nearly all pathogen populations regardless of whether they supported coinfection or not (96% vs. 93%, respectively).
source: Resting spores, which were visually scored in the field (Tack and Laine, 2014), were produced in nearly all pathogen populations regardless of whether they supported coinfection or not (96% vs. 93%, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding based on field observations, with a citation for the method.

claim: Spatial variation in coinfection results in spatially delineated hotspots of novel genetic diversity.
source: We find that spatial variation in coinfection results in spatially delineated hotspots of novel genetic diversity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: The high number of new MLGs detected every year is indicative of outcrossing taking place in this pathogen metapopulation.
source: The high number of new MLGs detected every year is indicative of outcrossing taking place in this pathogen metapopulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on novel MLGs.

claim: Sampling is likely to miss some rare strains.
source: Although our sampling is likely to miss some rare strains, and novel MLGs may be generated through mutations, these are unlikely to explain the high turnover of MLGs between years we report here.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of potential limitations in the sampling approach.

claim: Mainland populations are expected to play a negligible role as sources of gene flow given that experimental and field data have confirmed this pathogen to typically disperse short distances.
source: Mainland populations, which are separated by at least 38 km of open water, are also expected to play a negligible role as sources of gene flow given that experimental and field data have confirmed this pathogen to typically disperse short distances (Jousimo et al., 2014; Tack et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior work on dispersal.

claim: Sexual outcrossing takes place where there is the opportunity for it, that is in populations where levels of coinfection are high.
source: Our results suggest that sexual outcrossing takes place where there is the opportunity for it, that is in populations where levels of coinfection are high.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: This phenomenon has only received limited experimentally derived support in pathogens.
source: To date, this phenomenon has only received limited experimentally derived support in pathogens (Schelkle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Generation of novel genetic diversity may increase transmission across host populations that support considerable resistance diversity both within and among populations.
source: In the short term, generation of novel genetic diversity may increase transmission across host populations that support considerable resistance diversity both within and among populations (Jousimo et al., 2014; Laine et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation about the consequences of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Novel genetic diversity may also increase the evolutionary potential of pathogens that need to adapt to both biotic and abiotic variation in their environment.
source: Novel genetic diversity may also increase the evolutionary potential of pathogens that need to adapt to both biotic and abiotic variation in their environment (Greischar and Koskella, 2007; Wolinska and King, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation about the consequences of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Overwintering determines both the genetic and numeric structure of the next epidemic.
source: Overwintering determines both the genetic and numeric structure of the next epidemic (Tack and Laine, 2014; Penczykowski et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Successful overwintering is not due to higher production of resting spores.
source: Our results suggest that successful overwintering is not due to higher production of resting spores.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing similar resting spore production in populations with and without coinfection.

claim: There may be a difference in the quality of progeny produced via selfing vs. outcrossing.
source: Hence, there may be a difference in the quality of progeny produced via selfing vs. outcrossing.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the finding that overwintering success differs despite similar resting spore production.

claim: Prior experimental work has demonstrated significant variation in spore viability in the resting structures of P. plantaginis.
source: Prior experimental work has demonstrated significant variation in spore viability in the resting structures of P. plantaginis.
evidence: This is a statement about prior experimental work.

claim: There is evidence of higher viability of progeny from coinfections than from single infections, but the strength and direction of this trend is affected by the genotypes of the interacting strains, as well as by temperature.
source: There is evidence of higher viability of progeny from coinfections than from single infections, but the strength and direction of this trend is affected by the genotypes of the interacting strains, as well as by temperature (Vaumourin and Laine, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Haploid selfing may be preserved due to the low probability of encountering a suitable mating partner infecting the same host.
source: Despite the higher overwintering success of outcrossed progeny, haploid selfing may be preserved due to the low probability of encountering a suitable mating partner infecting the same host.
evidence: This is a speculation about the maintenance of selfing.

claim: There may be a cost to outcrossing as it breaks up locally adapted pathogen populations by producing novel – and potentially maladapted – genetic variation.
source: Moreover, there may be a cost to outcrossing as it breaks up locally adapted pathogen populations by producing novel – and potentially maladapted – genetic variation.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential costs of outcrossing.

claim: A loss of sexual reproduction in pathogens has been linked to homogenous habitat.
source: A loss of sexual reproduction in pathogens has been linked to homogenous habitat (Saleh et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A loss of sexual reproduction in pathogens has been linked to stable environmental conditions.
source: or stable environmental conditions (Barrett et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Maintaining a mixed mating system may provide a bet-hedging strategy for this pathogen to survive in a fragmented landscape, with a high probability of population extinction during the off-season.
source: Maintaining a mixed mating system may provide a bet-hedging strategy for this pathogen to survive in a fragmented landscape, with a high probability of population extinction during the off-season.
evidence: This is a speculation about the adaptive significance of the mixed mating system.

claim: Plantago lanceolata is a perennial rosette-forming herb that is naturally infected by Podosphaera plantaginis.
source: Plantago lanceolata is a perennial rosette-forming herb that is naturally infected by Podosphaera plantaginis (Castagne; U. Braun and S. Takamatsu), a powdery mildew fungus in the order Erysiphales within the Ascomycota.
evidence: This is a factual description of the study system based on established knowledge.

claim: Podosphaera plantaginis is a host-specific obligate biotroph that completes its entire life cycle on the surface of the host plant where it is visible as localized (nonsystemic) white powdery lesions.
source: This pathogen is a host-specific obligate biotroph that completes its entire life cycle on the surface of the host plant where it is visible as localized (nonsystemic) white powdery lesions.
evidence: This is a factual description of the pathogen based on established knowledge.

claim: The interaction between P. lanceolata and P. plantaginis functions in a two-step manner typical of many plant–pathogen associations.
source: The interaction between P. lanceolata and P. plantaginis functions in a two-step manner typical of many plant–pathogen associations.
evidence: This is a description of the interaction based on established knowledge.

claim: As the pathogen attempts to infect a new host, the interaction is strain specific as a given host genotype expresses resistance against some strains (recognition) of the pathogen while being susceptible to others (nonrecognition).
source: First, as the pathogen attempts to infect a new host, the interaction is strain specific as a given host genotype expresses resistance against some strains (recognition) of the pathogen while being susceptible to others (nonrecognition) (Jones and Dangl, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on plant-pathogen interactions.

claim: Once a P. plantaginis strain has successfully established there is still considerable variation in its development that is affected by both pathogen and host genotype.
source: Once a P. plantaginis strain has successfully established there is still considerable variation in its development that is affected by both pathogen and host genotype (Laine, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The pathogen is a significant stress factor for its host and may cause host mortality.
source: The pathogen is a significant stress factor for its host and may cause host mortality (Penczykowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The locations of P. lanceolata populations have been systematically mapped in the Åland Islands, southwest of Finland, since the 1990s.
source: The locations of P. lanceolata populations have been systematically mapped in the Åland Islands, southwest of Finland, since the 1990s.
evidence: This is a description of the long-term study system.

claim: There are currently c. 4000 known host populations that range in size from a few square meters to several hectares, with a median size of 300 m2.
source: There are currently c. 4000 known host populations that range in size from a few square meters to several hectares, with a median size of 300 m2 (Jousimo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the study system supported by a citation.

claim: Within host populations, initial pathogen foci are established from resting spores (chasmothecia), or from a spore immigrating into the local population from another population.
source: Within host populations, initial pathogen foci are established from resting spores (chasmothecia), or from a spore immigrating into the local population from another population.
evidence: This is a description of the pathogen life cycle based on established knowledge.

claim: The first visible signs of infection appear in late June as white-greyish lesions consisting of mycelium supporting spores (conidia) are formed.
source: The first visible signs of infection appear in late June as white-greyish lesions consisting of mycelium supporting spores (conidia) are formed.
evidence: This is a description of the pathogen life cycle based on field observations.

claim: Some six to eight clonally produced generations follow one another in quick succession, often leading to a substantial proportion of the host individuals within a population being infected by late summer.
source: Some six to eight clonally produced generations (estimated from spore germination-production times observed in the laboratory) follow one another in quick succession, often leading to a substantial proportion of the host individuals within a population being infected by late summer (Ovaskainen and Laine, 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the pathogen life cycle supported by a citation.

claim: Resting spores (chasmothecia) appear towards the end of the growing season in August–September.
source: Resting spores (chasmothecia) appear towards the end of the growing season in August–September.
evidence: This is a description of the pathogen life cycle based on field observations.

claim: Each chasmothecia contains eight ascospores that can each cause a new infection in the spring upon their release.
source: Each chasmothecia contains eight ascospores that can each cause a new infection in the spring upon their release.
evidence: This is a description of the pathogen life cycle based on established knowledge.

claim: Infected leaves may support hundreds of chasmothecia.
source: Infected leaves may support hundreds of chasmothecia.
evidence: This is a description based on field observations.

claim: Pure strains of P. plantaginis have been shown to carry both MAT1-1-1 and MAT1-2-1 that determine compatibility in several other powdery mildew species.
source: Pure strains of P. plantaginis have been shown to carry both MAT1-1-1 and MAT1-2-1 that determine compatibility in several other powdery mildew species (Tollenaere and Laine, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In early September every year since 2001, all known P. lanceolata populations have been surveyed for the presence/absence of the powdery mildew.
source: In early September every year since 2001, all known P. lanceolata populations have been surveyed for the presence/absence of the powdery mildew (for details on the survey, please see Jousimo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the survey methods with a citation for details.

claim: Survey data can be used to identify pathogen populations which have persisted from one year to the next, newly colonized populations, and populations that have gone extinct.
source: These data can be used to identify pathogen populations, which have persisted from one year to the next, newly colonized populations, and populations that have gone extinct.
evidence: This is a description of how the survey data are used.

claim: In 2012–15 nearly all located pathogen populations were sampled for genotyping (N = 619, 703, 693, and 833 populations, respectively, which represented 96–97% of all located pathogen populations each year).
source: In 2012–15 nearly all located pathogen populations were sampled for genotyping (N = 619, 703, 693, and 833 populations, respectively, which represented 96–97% of all located pathogen populations each year; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the sampling effort.

claim: A sample consists of one infected leaf collected from an infected plant, and infected plants were sampled at a minimum distance of five meters between infected plants.
source: A sample consists of one infected leaf collected from an infected plant, and infected plants were sampled at a minimum distance of five meters between infected plants.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling protocol.

claim: The aim was to collect ten samples from each population but in smaller pathogen populations sampling effort needed to be scaled to how much infection was available for sampling.
source: The aim was to collect ten samples from each population but in smaller pathogen populations sampling effort needed to be scaled to how much infection was available for sampling
evidence: This is a description of the sampling protocol.

claim: DNA extraction was performed using E.Z.N.A. Plant DNA kit at The Institute of Biotechnology.
source: DNA extraction was performed using E.Z.N.A. Plant DNA kit (Omega Bio Tek Inc, Norcross, GA, USA) at The Institute of Biotechnology (BI, Helsinki, Finland).
evidence: This is a description of the laboratory methods.

claim: Samples were genotyped with 27 SNP markers using Sequenom MassARRAY iPLEX platform.
source: Samples were genotyped with 27 SNP markers using Sequenom MassARRAY iPLEX platform as described in Tollenaere et al. (2012) at the Finnish Institute for Molecular Medicine (FIMM, Helsinki, Finland).
evidence: This is a description of the genotyping methods with a citation.

claim: Eight SNP were discarded from the analysis because of the presence of null alleles in the studied populations.
source: Because of the presence of null alleles in the studied populations, eight SNP were discarded from the analysis.
evidence: This is a description of data filtering.

claim: Podosphaera plantaginis is haploid.
source: Podosphaera plantaginis is haploid, and therefore the detection of a heterozygote genotype for one or more SNP markers is a clear highly repeatable method for calling coinfections (Tollenaere et al., 2012; Susi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the ploidy of the pathogen supported by citations.

claim: The detection of a heterozygote genotype for one or more SNP markers is a clear highly repeatable method for calling coinfections in P. plantaginis.
source: Podosphaera plantaginis is haploid, and therefore the detection of a heterozygote genotype for one or more SNP markers is a clear highly repeatable method for calling coinfections (Tollenaere et al., 2012; Susi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the method for detecting coinfections supported by citations.

claim: Connectivity of pathogen populations is considered a proxy for gene flow among populations as it is estimated from distances separating local pathogen populations.
source: Connectivity of pathogen populations, which is considered a proxy for gene flow among populations as it is estimated from distances separating local pathogen populations (Jousimo et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a description of the connectivity measure supported by a citation.

claim: The parameter α, describing the mean dispersal distance at the metapopulation level, was set α=1000 (meters) following results of Jousimo et al. (2014).
source: The parameter α, describing the mean dispersal distance at the metapopulation level, was set α=1000 (meters) following results of Jousimo et al. (2014).
evidence: This is a description of a parameter value used in the analysis, based on prior work.

claim: Finding more coinfection than would be expected by chance is in line with previous fine-scale field sampling of infections and experimental work, which show that hosts already infected with one strain of the pathogen are more likely to become infected by another strain of the same pathogen than uninfected hosts.
source: Finding more coinfection than would be expected by chance is in line with previous fine-scale field sampling of infections and experimental work, which show that hosts already infected with one strain of the pathogen are more likely to become infected by another strain of the same pathogen than uninfected hosts (Laine, 2011; Susi and Laine, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Already infected individuals may become more susceptible to subsequent infection.
source: This may be due to already infected individuals becoming more susceptible to subsequent infection, or due to strains aggregating on those hosts that are the most susceptible genotypes (Susi and Laine, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation about mechanisms supported by a citation.

claim: Strains may aggregate on those hosts that are the most susceptible genotypes.
source: This may be due to already infected individuals becoming more susceptible to subsequent infection, or due to strains aggregating on those hosts that are the most susceptible genotypes (Susi and Laine, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation about mechanisms supported by a citation.

claim: Variation in host density and (micro)climatic conditions may be an important driver of infection patterns in the wild.
source: Moreover, variation in host density and (micro)climatic conditions may be an important driver of infection patters in the wild (Penczykowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation.

claim: The results do not support the priming hypothesis, whereby prior attack provides increased protection against later attack.
source: Our results do not support the priming hypothesis (Hilker et al., 2016), whereby prior attack provides increased protection against later attack.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data, with a citation for the priming hypothesis.

claim: Coinfection is the prerequisite for sex in this pathogen.
source: Populations supporting high levels of coinfection –a prerequisite of sex – result in hotspots of novel genetic diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is based on the biology of the pathogen where outcrossing requires two strains infecting the same host.

claim: Outcrossing has direct epidemiological consequences in this pathogen system.
source: Jointly our results show that outcrossing has direct epidemiological consequences as well as a major impact on pathogen population genetic diversity, thereby providing evidence of ecological and evolutionary benefits of outcrossing in pathogens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: Outcrossing has a major impact on pathogen population genetic diversity.
source: Jointly our results show that outcrossing has direct epidemiological consequences as well as a major impact on pathogen population genetic diversity, thereby providing evidence of ecological and evolutionary benefits of outcrossing in pathogens.
